questiontext.text: Why do neural large language models frequently recognize archaic spellings (such as 18th-century French -oit or English shew'd) that cause deterministic lookup taggers to fail?

answer.text: Because their massive pre-training data incorporates centuries of digitized historical books and archival literature.

answer.text: Because LLMs are programmed with every rule of 18th-century grammar by human linguists.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neural models learn statistical associations from massive corpora rather than manual rule coding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pre-training exposure across historical text is what supplies morphological familiarity.

feedback.text: Correct. Explicitly providing the tagset ensures interoperability and prevents models from mixing legacy tagsets like Penn Treebank.

generalfeedback.text: Negative constraints prevent AI models from modernizing historical spellings, dropping punctuation, or adding conversational filler.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative constraints are linguistic rules, not display configurations.

name.text: 06 Question: Invented word Modes in Historical Lemmatization

answer.text: A plausible-sounding but factually non-existent headword invented by the model rather than found in an authoritative lexicon.

answer.text: A genuine historical word that human editors have forgotten how to read.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A verified headword is authentic ground truth, not an invented hallucination.

generalfeedback.text: Classify every disagreement into Category A (human slip), B (NLP rigid miss), C (AI hallucination), or D (genuine crux).
